planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions in consistently moist to wet soil in spring; this species spreads aggressively by both seed and rooting stolons, so site it where it can be contained.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to boggy soil in partial shade to full sun, where its glossy, buttercup-yellow flowers appear from late spring through summer. The species spreads rapidly by creeping stolons that root at each node, making it useful as a tough wet-soil groundcover but prone to escaping bounds in garden beds. Divide crowded clumps in spring or fall, and shear or mow after bloom to control spread in lawns and damp meadow areas. Avoid planting near cultivated beds unless contained, as it readily naturalizes in ditches, pond margins, and poorly drained turf.
sources: Oregon State University Extension -- Creeping Buttercup

common_name: Aconite-Leaf Buttercup (Wild Fair Maids of France)

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade; this clump-forming buttercup relative does not spread by runners like most of its genus.

directions: Grow in reliably moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, ideally along a stream bank or pond edge where its wiry, branched stems carry small white single flowers above deeply divided foliage in late spring. Unlike the stoloniferous Ranunculus repens, this European alpine meadow species forms a neat, non-invasive clump that associates well with ferns and hostas. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor, and keep soil from drying out during summer, since it declines quickly in dry conditions. It is the wild, single-flowered parent species behind the better-known double 'Flore Pleno' selection found in cottage gardens.

subcategory: moisture-loving perennial for bog and pond margins

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into rich, consistently moist soil; this species tolerates boggy ground better than most perennials and resents drying out even briefly.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in heavy, continuously moist to wet soil, such as along a pond edge or low garden spot that stays damp through summer. Tall, wiry stems carry bright orange-yellow globe-shaped flowers with twisted, overlapping petals held well above glossy, deeply cut foliage in early to midsummer. This East Asian species is the taller, later-blooming counterpart to the European Trollius europaeus and the parent of many garden hybrids sold under T. x cultorum. Mulch to retain soil moisture and divide every three to four years in spring as clumps become congested.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Himalayan species spreads steadily by underground rhizomes to form a dense weed-smothering mat.

directions: Grow in average garden soil with reliable drainage in full sun or light afternoon shade, where this Himalayan cranesbill spreads by creeping rhizomes into a low, weed-suppressing mat of lobed foliage. Violet-blue, dark-veined flowers appear over a long early to midsummer season above the deeply cut leaves. It is the wild species behind the popular Kashmir hybrid cultivars and performs best where summers are not excessively hot and humid. Cut back hard after the main flush of bloom to tidy the foliage and encourage a lighter rebloom into late summer.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out plants after the last frost in average, well-drained soil in sun to light shade; this species self-seeds freely and naturalizes readily in informal plantings.

directions: Plant in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade, where it quickly forms a loose, airy clump of rounded, lobed leaves topped with small notch-petaled pink-purple flowers from late spring through summer. This European species is short-lived but compensates by self-seeding generously, making it a reliable gap-filler in cottage and cutting gardens once established. It tolerates poor soil and light drought once rooted in, and deadheading spent flower stems reduces unwanted self-sowing if a tidier look is desired. Established plants can be divided in early spring if a particular seedling's color is worth preserving.

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plants in spring in average to rich, well-drained soil in full sun; this larger-leaved catmint tolerates a bit more moisture than smaller Nepeta species.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in average, well-drained garden soil, where its coarsely toothed, deep green foliage and tall whorled spikes of violet-blue flowers anchor the middle of a mixed perennial border through summer. This Caucasus native is larger in leaf and flower than the familiar Nepeta cataria and Nepeta x faassenii, and it is the wild species behind named selections such as 'Bramdean' and 'Dawn to Dusk'. Shear stems back hard after the first bloom flush to keep growth dense and prompt renewed flowering into early autumn. Once established it tolerates dry spells well and is rarely bothered by deer or rabbits.

planting.note: Sow seed indoors with 4-6 weeks of cold, moist stratification before starting at room temperature, since fresh seed germinates slowly and erratically without a chill period; transplant after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; this European Alps native produces intricate, steely-blue thistle-like flowerheads surrounded by finely cut, feathery silver-blue bracts in mid to late summer. It is one of the showiest sea hollies, often grown as the species behind the popular 'Superbum' selection, and dried stems hold their color well for winter arrangements. Established plants resent being disturbed, so site them carefully and avoid dividing; instead, propagate by root cuttings or fresh seed. Heavy clay or wet winter soil is its chief enemy and will quickly rot the deep taproot.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants develop a deep taproot and resent later transplanting.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, where this Balkan native sends up stiff, silvery-stemmed spikes topped with perfectly round, steel-blue flowerheads from mid to late summer. Bees and other pollinators work the globe-shaped flowers heavily, and the spent heads can be left standing for winter interest or cut for dried arrangements. It is highly drought-tolerant once established and is the wild species behind the widely sold 'Blue Globe' and similar named selections. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages floppy growth and shortens the plant's lifespan.
